clue.text: Number 1 (not very hard) on a scale of mental challenges …

definitions.text: Number 1 (not very hard) on a scale

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the phrase that follows, so 'of' points inside those two words

explanation.surface: An ellipsis-led puzzle note: some brainteaser is the easiest, number one, on a ranking of mental challenges.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'scale' is the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, which runs from 1 to 10; 'not very hard' is literal, not a comment on difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: On the Mohs hardness scale the softest mineral, rated 1, is talc.

clue.text: Hendry's first to break off — and remains here at table

indicators.note: the initial letter breaks into the other word, splitting it open

parts.note: gone off course means gone astray

indicators.note: first signals only the opening letter of the snooker player's name

explanation.surface: Snooker: Stephen Hendry breaks off, and the remains are left on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Hendry was a snooker champion, so 'break off' and 'table' suggest the opening shot, but the table is where you sit and the remains are cigarette ash.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish at the table where smokers leave their ash and stubs is that receptacle.

clue.text: Juicy pairings, did you say? These linkups involve more than two

definitions.meaning: spoken, 'pairings' is 'pear rings': a juicy Conference pear (a British variety) and rings, telephone calls

definitions.text: These linkups involve more than two
definitions.meaning: telephone or video meetings joining three or more parties

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether juicy pairings were meant, then explains linkups with more than two parties.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'pairings' and it becomes 'pear rings'. Conference is a common British pear variety; rings, as in phone rings, are calls. No single clue word maps to letters, so this reads as two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A telephone or video meeting connecting three or more parties at once is such a call.

clue.text: Loss, say, of poor swimmer who drowned relocating north

indicators.note: one letter is shifted to a new place within the word, so it is relocated

parts.note: poor in quality means bad
Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to Hero and drowned in a storm
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: An obituary note: the loss of a weak swimmer who drowned while moving north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loss' is not grief but Joe Loss, a British dance-band leader. 'Relocating north' moves the N of BADLEANDER to after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Loss led a famous British big band, so he is an example of one who conducts a band.

clue.text: Generally agreed Apennines must range across Italy in part

indicators.note: the shuffled mountains are placed inside the word for a piece

parts.note: a bit is a part or piece

indicators.note: to range is to wander about, so the mountain letters are rearranged
the anagram reaches across the I of the outer word, using that I as Italy's letter rather than a second one

parts.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: A geography fact: the Apennines are agreed to run across part of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of APENNINES spans the I in BIT, sharing it: B, I, then ENPENSAN (the rest of 'Apennines', shuffled by 'must range'), then T.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase describes opinions held by right-thinking people, conventionally accepted views.

clue.text: Ancient Orpington out of bounds?

parts.note: read as 'out of leaps': having no bounds means having no spring
the Orpington is a breed of domestic fowl

explanation.surface: An old Orpington hen has strayed beyond the farm limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of bounds' normally means forbidden territory; here it means having run out of bounces. An Orpington is a British breed of hen.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone no longer young, so it serves for very old.

clue.text: Too old to get up (locked in lav)

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means the letters climb, reading upward
the letters sit locked inside the words that come before

explanation.surface: An elderly person, too old to stand, is stuck locked in the lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Lav and the other short word are both informal British names for the toilet.

clue.text: Man endlessly out rocking with 4 Across stars

indicators.note: rocking shakes things about, so the gathered letters are mixed
the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: the cross-reference points to the earlier answer, a dance-band conductor

explanation.surface: A man is out rocking with a bandleader and his star performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' trims OUT to OU; MAN, OU and the 4 Across answer are then shuffled by 'rocking'.
explanation.definitionFit: The great spiral galaxy in Andromeda is a vast system of stars, once called a nebula.

clue.text: Ability to pick up French players in the first few minutes

parts.note: having an ear for music is an ability to pick things up by listening
Olympique Lyonnais, the football club, play in Lyon

explanation.surface: A talent scout notes a French team's skill at picking up the ball early in the match.
explanation.walkthrough: Lyon is a French city whose football club is a regular in Ligue 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening soon after the start of a match or period happens at an initial stage.

clue.text: Such as upset Beaujolais Nouveau through inept clownishness?

definitions.text: Such as upset Beaujolais Nouveau through inept clownishness?

indicators.note: one piece is pushed through the middle of the other
clumsy and unskilled, so the letters are bungled into a new order
knocked over, so the wine word is turned backwards

parts.note: this young French wine is a red

explanation.surface: Pictures upper-class buffoons knocking over the new Beaujolais through clumsy foolery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' turns RED into DER, which goes through the anagram of CLOWNISHNESS made by 'inept'. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeble, upper-class young men stereotyped as foolish and weak-jawed are exactly the kind to topple a wine glass by clumsiness.

clue.text: An Independent whisky giveaway?

definitions.meaning: a person who goes their own way, free of convention
whisky is a spirit, and one given away costs nothing

explanation.surface: The newspaper offers its readers a bottle of whisky for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Independent' is capitalised to suggest the newspaper that published the puzzle; it means an independent-minded person.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonconformist living by their own rules is called this, and a complimentary dram is literally the phrase.

clue.text: Something perhaps ironic about cross old media mogul's Hall?

indicators.note: the first piece goes about, around, the second

parts.note: irony is one example of a figure of speech, a trope
a cross between breeds is a hybrid

explanation.surface: Something ironic about an angry old media tycoon's hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Hall is Jerry Hall, the model who married Rupert Murdoch, the elderly media magnate; 'cross' is a noun, not anger.
explanation.definitionFit: A young or glamorous wife seen as a status prize for a rich older man; the question mark marks Hall as an example.

clue.text: Its bands are in black and white half of New York Times

definitions.text: Its bands are in black and white

indicators.note: half of a two-letter word is its first letter

parts.note: x is the multiplication sign, read as times

explanation.surface: A newspaper note: its stripes are in black and white, half the New York Times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New York Times' is a newspaper in the surface; here it splits into NY and X, and 'half of' takes the O of 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: This banded chalcedony gemstone typically shows alternating black and white layers.

clue.text: Awfully nervy on the trail of Welsh monster

indicators.note: following behind, so the shuffled letters come after the abbreviation
badly or terribly, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone terribly nervous is tracking a Welsh monster.
explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh dragon fits the surface, but 'Welsh' is only the letter W at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-legged winged dragon of heraldry and legend is a mythical beast.

clue.text: Teary aye-aye almost caught by grandmother

indicators.note: the shortened phrase is held inside the word for granny

parts.note: nan is a familiar British word for grandmother

indicators.note: drop the final letter of the sailor's reply

parts.note: a sailor's 'aye aye' is a promise to obey orders: I obey

explanation.surface: A tearful lemur is nearly grabbed by an old woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The aye-aye is a lemur in the surface, but 'aye aye' is what a sailor says to mean 'I obey'. Niobe of Greek myth wept endlessly for her slain children.
explanation.definitionFit: Like Niobe, the weeping mother of myth, describes someone inconsolably tearful.

clue.text: Old fashioned seat on cycle covered by bill

indicators.note: the inner part sits under the cover of the outer abbreviation

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill

indicators.note: letters go round, the last one moved to the front

parts.note: a chair is a seat

explanation.surface: An old-style bicycle seat is paid for with a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On cycle' looks like a bicycle saddle but moves the final R of CHAIR to the front, making RCHAI.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiquated or belonging to an earlier era, out of date in style.

clue.text: Mexican native not entirely eloquent when gate-crashing a party

indicators.note: the shortened word pushes its way into the party pieces uninvited

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: the final letter is dropped

parts.note: vocal means outspoken or eloquent

explanation.surface: A Mexican, not wholly articulate, gatecrashes a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native' suggests a person, but the native here is a fruit that originated in Mexico.
explanation.definitionFit: This pear-shaped green fruit tree is indigenous to Mexico and Central America.

clue.text: Means to move body, head having been extracted from buttocks

indicators.note: the leading letter is pulled out of the phrase

parts.note: the arse is crude British slang for the buttocks

explanation.surface: A crude image of something being pulled out of someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' looks anatomical but is a corpse; ARSE is British slang for the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral vehicle carries a coffin and corpse to burial.

clue.text: Reaction to winter wind, ice and snow flakes

definitions.meaning: trembling with cold is the body's response to an icy wind
small fragments or splinters, as when ice is shattered

explanation.surface: Describes a winter day of wind, ice and falling snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flakes' looks like snowflakes but means slivers or splinters, an old sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Trembles from cold, and also fragments or slivers of something shattered.

clue.text: Twisted band of gold — not silvery metal — at first light

indicators.note: one metal is taken instead of the other, gold and not aluminium

parts.note: the first light is the opening entry of the grid, 1 Across, a soft mineral
Al is the chemical symbol for aluminium, a silvery metal
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A twisted band of gold, not silver, seen at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first light' suggests dawn, but a light is a grid entry: the first one, 1 Across. In it, gold (OR) replaces aluminium (AL).
explanation.definitionFit: A neck ring of twisted metal worn by ancient Celts is a twisted band.

clue.text: Shifty blighter pinching Nimrod's trick

indicators.note: the shuffled letters grab hold of the short piece, enclosing it
shifting letters about, so this word is an anagram cue

parts.note: Nimrod is the setter, so 'Nimrod's' stands for I'm

explanation.surface: A shady rogue is stealing the setter's trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nimrod's' is the setter speaking: Nimrod is = I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: The three-cups-and-a-pea swindle is a sleight-of-hand con, a trick.

clue.text: Improv quotes from the likes of Yogi Berra?

definitions.meaning: rough, improvised price quotes or estimates
Yogi Berra was a baseball catcher, a figure of the ballpark

explanation.surface: Collects off-the-cuff sayings of Yogi Berra, the famously quotable baseball player.
explanation.walkthrough: Yogi Berra's quotes seem the point, but 'quotes' are price estimates, and Berra is just an example of a baseball player.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough approximate numbers, and literally notable people of the baseball park.

clue.text: One must have at least — surely — some 22?

definitions.text: One must have at least — surely — some 22?

parts.note: a is the indefinite article, meaning one

indicators.note: only the least part of each word, the initial letter, is used

explanation.surface: Asks whether every being must surely have at least some common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is HORSE SENSE. A donkey, being equine, must have some horse in it, though it is proverbially foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: The donkey is a kind of horse relative, so it ought to possess some equine wit.

clue.text: "Nous serons" she translated with only a little English

indicators.note: translation turns words into a new form, so the letters are rearranged
just the opening letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A French sentence, 'we will be', is translated with barely any English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nous' looks like French 'we' but is the English word for common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is British informal for practical good judgment or common sense.

clue.text: … and more exceptional solving cases

indicators.note: the two words act as cases holding the letters inside them

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 Across: and more exceptional cases of solving.
explanation.definitionFit: Also adds something further, in addition, just like 'and more'.
